867K likes, 12K comments - figuringout.co on September 1, 2026: "Comment ‘Andrew’ and we’ll personally DM you the full conversation.

What’s the one habit you struggle most to stay consistent with?

In today’s episode, we sit down with Andrew Huberman, professor & neuroscientist at Stanford and host of @hubermanlab, to unpack the science behind building a mind that performs under pressure and never collapses when it matters most.

Here’s what we discussed:
-Building a Stronger Mind: The daily habits that can help you become mentally resilient over the long term.
-Engineering Your Morning: How your morning routine, cortisol rhythm, and light exposure influence energy and focus.
-Mastering Pressure & Anxiety: Why we freeze under pressure and how to train yourself to take action anyway.
-The Long Game of Success: A three-phase approach to building consistency, discipline, and lasting success.
-What Makes Winners Different: Why successful people experience the same setbacks and despair but respond differently.

Catch the full episode here:
YouTube Channel: Raj Shamani
Spotify Channel: Raj Shamani Figuring Out

Until then, keep figuring out! 🚀

#rajshamani #figuringout".

76K likes, 706 comments - hubermanlab on September 15, 2026: "THE AGITATION FROM ERRORS THAT ACCOMPANIES YOUR GENUINE ATTEMPTS TO DO SOMETHING NEW ARE WHAT TRIGGER NEUROPLASTICITY & LEARNING •

Excerpt from @joerogan @joeroganexperience podcast out now @spotifypodcasts where we discussed how (and why, at a biological level) doing hard things makes doing other hard things feel easier, let’s you access more appreciation and leads to a sense of peace. 

We also discussed how some degree of frustration from making errors while trying to learn is a *necessary* component of stable learning. 

Most people back away from that agitation. But it literally reflects the release of neuromodulators that tell your brain connections to change. 

Understanding this fact can help you learn anything faster. Recognize what the agitation is and that, in the context of learning, it’s a good thing. You don’t want to be overly stressed, but you need to be agitated and focused on the task at hand. And making errors through genuine attempts. 

Forget learning in a flow state. There is no learning in flow and there is no flow in learning. Flow is the expression of what you already can do.

Our discussion also covered mental health from different perspectives, why it took me eight years and four complete rewrites before finally releasing my book Protocols, and much more.

Thank you, Joe for hosting me and for your questions and the discussion, and for your support all these years. 

Also, thank you @jamievernon and team for all you do to make the JRE what it is. Much gratitude.

You can find the podcast @spotifypodcasts @spotify as well as other places podcast are found.

Thank you for your interest in science!".

20K likes, 248 comments - hubermanlab on October 30, 2026: "WHEN TO *NOT* TRUST YOUR THOUGHTS

During my recent podcast discussion with @rossedgley about motivation and how to access it using many mindsets — not just one, we arrived at the topic of circadian (cyclical) influences on mindset. 

The major takeaway of that portion of podcast is this: the longer you have been awake and in particular when you are awake between the hours of 2 AM and 5 AM (this is assuming you are diurnal) your forebrain is not very good at regulating the aspects of your brain controlling emotionality, rationality, and strategic decision-making. 

A different way to put this: you are seriously brain impaired during those hours. 

Again, if you’re nocturnal because you work the night shift this is not the case for that 2 AM to 5 AM stretch but it is true for most people who follow a sleep-wake schedule of asleep sometime between 9pm and 12midnight and wake up 5-8am.

So rather than despair about the thoughts that you have if you wake up in the middle of the night or worse— rather than making important decisions on the basis of those thoughts, understand that if you wait 4 to 6 hours (and ideally get some more sleep!) you’ll be significantly sharper, physically stronger and significantly more durable in both mind and body…

… and therefore able to make far better decisions.

This might seem like simple advice. Or even common sense. But most people don’t realize that their brain just doesn’t function well at those hours, and therefore trusting your thoughts in those hours is not a good idea. Unless you have to in an emergency, of course.

The brain is a wonderful organ, but just like many aspects of our biology, not all of its features are adaptive. I thought they come to you when you wake in the middle of the night our altered because of circadian mechanisms. 

Listen to your thoughts accordingly. Lend weight to them accordingly. Make decisions on the basis of them accordingly.

And speaking of thoughts, let me know yours about this topic, whatever they may be. Put them in the comments section below. 

Thank you for your interest in science!".

Unlocking Persistent Motivation & Extreme Resilience | with  @rossedgley 

My guest on the Huberman lab podcast out today is Ross Edgley — a British ultra-endurance athlete and author known for completing extraordinary athletic feats by tapping into diverse sources of motivation and resilience. 

We discuss the psychological and biological forces that allow people to persevere through extreme challenges. 

Then we cover how to dynamically update your sense of purpose, emotions, philosophy, and personal narratives to expand your ability to overcome adversity of all kinds. We also discuss the brain circuits and science of fatigue and stress adaptation. 

Ultimately, a new framework emerges that you can use to access persistent motivation.

155K likes, 1,563 comments - natureismetal on October 13, 2026: "DOPAMINE, SURPRISE & “THE ONE THAT GOT AWAY”•

✍️ by @hubermanlab

Being in pursuit of something and especially, being right on the cusp of obtaining a reward is a very strong stimulus for dopamine release in the brain. But perhaps the greatest stimulus of all for dopamine release is when that is followed by positive surprise. - The name for it is “reward prediction error”.

When we anticipate a reward, and it is not obtained or is smaller than what we expected, our baseline level of dopamine drops below what it was prior to the entire pursuit. Eventually it returns to normal. But we learn something about the value of the pursuit that preceded that lower reward from the dopamine changes (aka dynamics).

This video was shot during my lab’s an expedition with @michaelmuller7 to collect footage of great white sharks for a fear/anxiety VR stimulus @stanfordmed - We wanted tuna for our dinner and we had one on the line… we were expecting a (meal) reward. A local great white reminded us that, when they are around, humans eat last.

However, the reward of seeing it breach was greater than the meal we would’ve had. - I’ll also never forget that incident because when we get a big and unexpected release of dopamine, it leaves an indelible mark on our memory. - You can start to see why dopamine is so fundamental to the evolution of every species. **It’s the chemical currency that tells us about the value of our experiences and efforts**.".

9,928 likes, 736 comments - hubermanlab on October 19, 2026: "Comment LIFE and I’ll DM you a link to the full episode:
What Makes Great Leaders & How to Live an Extraordinary Life | with Dr. Jared Diamond

My guest on the Huberman Lab podcast out now is Dr. Jared Diamond, PhD, Pulitzer Prize-winning author, physiologist, evolutionary biologist and Professor at UCLA. 

We discuss the surprising and often chance events that shaped human history and leadership in politics, religion, business and athletics. 

As one of the most influential public-facing scholars of the last 100 years, Dr. Diamond also shares his advice on how to pursue a career and life that reflects your unique interests and that makes a positive contribution to the world. 

He also shares the tools he uses to keep his mind and body vigorous. Jared speaks 13 languages (! fluently !) and has succeeded in many different areas of science and other career tracks.

He has a relentlessly “committed to curiosity” mindset and at just shy of 90 years old is still firing on all cylinders! 

Our discussion is one that will educate, dispel common myths about leaders and humans in general, and that no doubt will inspire you to be unabashedly yourself! 

Please put any questions or comments or suggestions of guests or topics you’d like me to cover on the podcast below and as always, thank you for your interest in science!

@stanford @stanford.med @ucla 
#neuroscience #science #ciencia #neurociencia #yourpath".

61K likes, 1,070 comments - hubermanlab on October 17, 2026: "The word addiction is thrown around a lot these days. It’s hard to separate the classic definition: “progressive use of a substance or behavior, despite detrimental effects to self or others” from the more modern definition/understanding (that more fully matches the underlying neuroscience): 

“causes a progressive narrowing of the things that bring you pleasure.” 

….but the same circuitry underlies both definitions. No matter the language one uses to describe it.

And there are healthy and unhealthy addictions. What’s the difference?

Healthy “addictions” tend to be ones that don’t limit pleasure for other things and wellbeing overall. They are benevolent. 

The opposite of addiction, in my opinion, has at least something to do with the progressive expansion of the things that bring you pleasure. Enlightenment is a complicated and squishy term. It’s not a scientific term. It’s not operationally defined. But I think we all sort of intuitively know what it means.

If you would like to add or edit anything to what is in this post, please do. It’s more about stimulating thought and discussion around these issues than planting a flag. 

I’m genuinely curious what people feel compelled to do —-healthy or unhealthy, these days.

Meanwhile, consider where your biology might’ve been hijacked, how to take control of it through conscious awareness, and above all, I do hope everyone will think about ways to expand their experience of healthy delight(s) in daily life.

Several upcoming episodes of the Huberman lab podcast deal specifically with these issues at the mechanistic and actionable level.

And as always, thank you for your interest in science!

@stanford @stanford.med 
#neuroscience #science #ciencia #neurociencia #driven".

26K likes, 491 comments - hubermanlab on October 15, 2026: "ENTRAINMENT GOVERNS YOUR ENERGY & FOCUS •

Entrainment is one of the most powerful aspects of our biology. 

Our circadian rhythm is created within us, but numerous studies show that our health is best when it is entrained to the rising and setting of the sun. That’s not to say you have to wake up at sunrise, but people who try to live nocturnally definitely suffer health consequences and people who match their sleep rhythm even somewhat to the rising and setting of the sun (one form of entrainment), derive many health benefits.

Entrainment works on shorter time scales too. Exercise at roughly the same time for a few days and you’ll notice your energy will increases a few minutes before that typical workout time.

Study or do some reading or some other form of work or learning at roughly the same time or times per day, and you’ll notice that your mental sharpness will start to increase in anticipation of those times.

To be clear, some of this is psychological, but a lot of it is physiological. The neuromodulators, hormones and neurotransmitters that regulate alertness and focus are readily susceptible to entrainment.

And entrainment is a concept that we can leverage. Not to make us rigid, but understanding it can help you make better sense of why you are more energetic and mentally sharp at particular times of day, and it can give you flexibility over what those times are.

Each of us has to follow a different schedule, but for me, because I like to get up early and get the dog walked and exercise early and then drop into work, I’ve noticed that my peak focus occurs first from 10 AM to 2PM, and then again between about 3 PM and 7 PM. And again 9-midnight. (But I  prefer to sleep by 10:30-11). That’s just me.

Figure out your schedule. You can leverage entrainment to get the most out of your workouts and work, etc. Two or three days on a regular schedule usually does the trick. No need to be overly rigid.

Please put any questions you have below and thank you for your interest in science!".

My guest on the Huberman Lab podcast out now is Dr. Scott Kanoski, PhD, Professor of Human and Evolutionary Biology and Neurobiology at the University of Southern California. 

We discuss how different foods impact memory and cognitive function as well as your cravings. 

We also discuss how GLP-1 drugs work to control hunger in the brain and body, the role of the gut microbiome, and the effects of artificial and low calorie sweeteners on hunger and satiety.

13K likes, 166 comments - hubermanlab on October 8, 2026: "SUCCESS IS DETERMINED BY HOW PRECISELY YOU MATCH YOUR GENUINE CURIOSITY TO THE WORK THAT YOU DO •

Obviously, here I’m talking about career success (but there are parallels to this in other areas of life). 

Also obvious is that we can’t always do the work that we would like to do most. There are practical considerations. 

But ultimately, if we want to make a living doing what we love most and do our very best work, it’s important we invest time in what we are most interested in seeing in the world and curious about.

This clip excerpt is from me as a guest on the podcast Invest With the Best. 

He asked me: “what is the kindest thing anyone has ever done for you?”

My answer was that Barbara Chapman, who eventually became my PhD advisor, had reminded me that the most important thing is to work on the things we are most curious about. And ignore any internal or external noise about what we should be doing instead.

Barbara and I went onto publish a lot of studies together. It was a ton of work, but we had so much fun doing those projects. In no small part because I was trying to answer the questions about the brain and brain development that were most burning for me at the time. 

Some years later, I shifted to working on other scientific questions (postdoc years) and then again (before tenure) and again (after tenure) and I eventually launched the Huberman Lab podcast. 

Because that’s where my curiosity went. Each stage worked out great. And there will be a next stage of interests at some point too. 

None of it came easy, but I’m so glad Barbara convinced me to follow my curiosity. Always. 

The takeaway is that whether field or career track is crowded or empty, if you follow your strongest curiosity, your motivation never flags (if you take care of yourself physically that is!) and you inevitably do your best work.

So once again, while there are practical considerations along one’s life and career track, when you can, follow your curiosity, even if it means going against the grain. 

I did. And I never looked back. And I’ll continue to do that going forward. 

My wish for everyone - for you, is that you do the same.".
